title: Unlock Faster Writes in Delta Lake with Deletion Vectors
summary: A technical community walkthrough of Delta Lake deletion vectors and their performance tradeoffs. The extracted claims explain merge-on-read mutation behavior, deletion-vector metadata, benchmark results, read overhead, OPTIMIZE requirements, and compatibility concerns for Fabric workloads.
audience: Fabric lakehouse engineers, Spark practitioners, and performance-focused architects working with Delta tables.
why_it_matters: Deletion vectors can reduce write amplification for mutation-heavy tables, but they introduce protocol compatibility and read-maintenance considerations. The source is useful for deciding when the feature improves net pipeline performance and when it creates downstream risk.
takeaways: Deletion vectors avoid rewriting entire Parquet files by recording row positions to filter at read time.
Write-heavy workloads can benefit, but read performance depends on regular OPTIMIZE maintenance.
Delta protocol version requirements can break unsupported downstream readers.
Fabric Copy Activity compatibility needs special caution when deletion vectors are enabled.

claims.text: Deletion vectors shift Delta Lake mutations from copy-on-write to merge-on-read: rather than rewriting entire Parquet files for any changed record, the system records the positions of affected rows in a small binary file and filters those rows out at query time.

Deletion vector metadata is stored as .bin files named with a UUID pattern; the Delta log entry for the affected Parquet file is annotated with storageType, path, offset, sizeInBytes, and cardinality fields pointing to the corresponding deletion vector file.

For UPDATE operations, deletion vectors soft-delete the old version of changed rows in their existing Parquet file via a new .bin record, then write only the updated row values to a new, smaller Parquet file — avoiding a full rewrite of the source file.

Enabling deletion vectors permanently raises a table's minReaderVersion to 3 and minWriterVersion to 7, requiring Delta reader/writer protocol version 2.3 or later; downstream consumers that do not support these versions will be unable to read the table.

In the author's benchmark against a 100-million-row synthetic dataset, deletion vectors reduced single-row delete time by roughly 8x, cut time for a 33% mass deletion by approximately 2.5x, sped up OPTIMIZE by about 2x, and reduced VACUUM duration by around 1.7x — with cumulative write-plus-maintenance time roughly halved compared to the baseline. These figures are from the author's controlled test and should be treated as directional.

Before running OPTIMIZE, deletion vectors produced about 3x less storage (2,351 MB versus 7,705 MB) and roughly 1.5x fewer files than the copy-on-write baseline in the author's benchmark, because soft-deletes avoid rewriting large unchanged files.

If deletion vectors accumulate without periodic OPTIMIZE, read performance degrades: the author's benchmark showed a scenario with 53% non-append changes and no compaction running 2.3x slower, and a MERGE-only scenario with 5M new records running 1.5x slower than the copy-on-write baseline.

After running OPTIMIZE to compact accumulated deletion vectors, read performance in the author's benchmark was identical between deletion-vector and copy-on-write tables, confirming that regular compaction eliminates the read overhead.

Deletion vectors are not suitable for tables consumed by Fabric COPY Activity: the feature is currently unsupported by that connector, and deleted or updated rows will reappear in the destination unless an OPTIMIZE is run immediately before each copy operation.

When the overall workflow includes regular OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, the author's benchmark found that deletion-vector tables had the lowest cumulative processing time across all operations, making the approach net-positive for write-heavy pipelines with proper maintenance.
